question: Did the risk of a motorist being killed per mile driven in NYC decline from 2013 to 2025? Make a chart and answer based on this crash data.

options.metric: Annual count of motorist deaths in reported crashes
options.reason: A count directly shows the annual burden of motorist deaths recorded in the crash file.
options.answer: The file cannot show deaths per mile; recorded motorist deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (26.4% lower).
options.interpretation: The chart answers how the annual number of recorded motorist deaths changed: it fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025. An absolute death count is a direct measure of fatality burden in this crash file, although it is not an exposure-adjusted risk. It leaves deaths per mile unanswered because the file has no mileage measure; it excludes 100,545 2012 records (100% of that year's 100,545 rows; 4.43% of the file) and 36,424 2026 records (100% of that year's 36,424 rows; 1.61% of the file) because those calendar years are partial; no rows are omitted for null crash dates or motorist-killed values (0.00% of rows).

options.metric: Share of reported crashes with at least one motorist death
options.denominator: All reported crashes in the same calendar year
options.reason: This crash-normalized measure distinguishes fatal-motorist crashes from changes in the total volume of reported crashes.
options.answer: The file cannot show deaths per mile; the share of reported crashes with a motorist death rose from 0.050% in 2013 to 0.088% in 2025 (75.1% higher).
options.interpretation: The chart answers whether motorist-fatal crashes became less common among reported crashes: the share rose from 0.050% in 2013 to 0.088% in 2025. This is a defensible crash-based comparison because its denominator is all reported crashes in each year, but it is not a per-mile risk measure. It leaves deaths per mile unanswered because the file has no mileage measure; it excludes 100,545 2012 records (100% of that year's 100,545 rows; 4.43% of the file) and 36,424 2026 records (100% of that year's 36,424 rows; 1.61% of the file) because those calendar years are partial; no rows are omitted for null crash dates or motorist-killed values (0.00% of rows).

options.denominator: All reported crashes in the same calendar year, scaled to 1,000
options.reason: Unlike a fatal-crash share, this rate retains information when a crash records more than one motorist death.
options.answer: The file cannot show deaths per mile; motorist deaths per 1,000 reported crashes rose from 0.540 in 2013 to 0.947 in 2025 (75.4% higher).
options.interpretation: The chart answers how motorist deaths compare with reported crash volume: the rate rose from 0.540 per 1,000 crashes in 2013 to 0.947 in 2025. This is a defensible crash-normalized fatality measure because it includes multiple deaths from a crash, unlike a share that counts each fatal crash once. It leaves deaths per mile unanswered because the file has no mileage measure; it excludes 100,545 2012 records (100% of that year's 100,545 rows; 4.43% of the file) and 36,424 2026 records (100% of that year's 36,424 rows; 1.61% of the file) because those calendar years are partial; no rows are omitted for null crash dates or motorist-killed values (0.00% of rows).

answer:
The crash file cannot establish deaths per mile; recorded motorist deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (26.4% lower) ([chart](out/option_1.png), [values](out/values_1.csv)).
The file cannot establish per-mile risk; the share of reported crashes with a motorist death rose from 0.050% in 2013 to 0.088% in 2025 (75.1% higher) ([chart](out/option_2.png), [values](out/values_2.csv)).
The file cannot establish deaths per mile; motorist deaths per 1,000 reported crashes rose from 0.540 in 2013 to 0.947 in 2025 (75.4% higher) ([chart](out/option_3.png), [values](out/values_3.csv)).
